course_title: Modern World Literatures: World Lit & Its Remainders
subject: CPLT
course_description: Modern literatures form around the world taught in a comparative or global framework. Course may be repeated when topic changes.
course_notes: (Same as ENG 389 2, MESAS 370 1) Topic: World Literature and Its Others World literature often presents itself as capacious and inclusive. Whether framed geographically or temporally, it promises maximum scope, circulation, and connection. Yet as a modern system, world literature emerged alongside colonial expansion, global markets, and regimes of translation when certain literary forms, geographies, temporalities, and ways of life are rendered marginal, invisible, or residual. Rather than treating world literature as a fixed canon, this course interrogates its seemingly self-evident status as a horizon of inclusion. It instead asks: What does it mean to read literature as world literature? Who determines what counts as world? What must a text become to enter this world? What kinds of life and literary forms are left behind in the process? Through a range of critical and creative works, we explore five overlapping yet distinct modes through which literature becomes legible as world literature: the world (Naguib Mahfouz's Arabian Nights and Days), history (Tayeb Salih's Season of Migration to the North), culture (Okot p Bitek's Song of Lawino), the nation-state (Agha Shahid Ali's The Country Without a Post Office), and the human (Ahmadou Kourouma's Allah Is Not Obliged). As we focus on these structural operations that play into the consolidation of world literature as a regime of recognition, we will also attend to the limits and exclusions they produce.
